evidence.text: ## User data on GitHub.com Here is a non-exhaustive list of the kinds of data we maintain about users and projects on GitHub. * **Public account data:** There is a variety of information publicly available on GitHub about users and their repositories. User profiles can be found at a URL such as `https://github.com/username`. User profiles display information about when the user created their account as well their public activity on GitHub.com and social interactions. Public user profiles can also include additional information that a user may have chosen to share publicly. All user public profiles display: * Username * The repositories that the user has starred * The other GitHub users the user follows * The users that follow them Optionally, a user may also choose to share the following information publicly: * Their real name * An avatar * An affiliated company * Their location * A public email address * Their personal web page * Organizations to which the user is a member (_depending on either the organizations' or the users' preferences_) * **Private account data:** GitHub also collects and maintains certain private information about users as outlined in our [Privacy Policy](/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-privacy-statement). This may include: * Private email addresses * Payment details * Security access logs * Data about interactions with private repositories To get a sense of the type of private account information that GitHub collects, you can visit your {% data reusables.user-settings.personal_dashboard %} and browse through the sections in the left-hand menubar. * **Organization account data:** Information about organizations, their administrative users and repositories is publicly available on GitHub. Organization profiles can be found at a URL such as `https://github.com/organization`. Public organization profiles can also include additional information that the owners have chosen to share publicly. All organization public profiles display: * The organization name * The repositories that the owners have starred * All GitHub users that are owners of the organization Optionally, administrative users may also choose to share the following information publicly: * An avatar * An affiliated company * Their location * Direct Members and Teams * Collaborators * **Public repository data:** GitHub is home to millions of public, open-source software projects. You can browse almost any public repository (for example, the [GitHub Docs](https://github.com/github/docs)) to get a sense for the information that GitHub collects and maintains about repositories. This can include: * The code itself * Previous versions of the code * Stable release versions of the project * Information about collaborators, contributors and repository members * Logs of Git operations such as commits, branching, pushing, pulling, forking and cloning * Conversations related to Git operations such as comments on pull requests or commits * Project documentation such as Issues and Wiki pages * Statistics and graphs showing contributions to the project and the network of contributors * **Private repository data:** GitHub collects and maintains the same type of data for private repositories that can be seen for public repositories, except only specifically invited users may access private repository data. * **Other data:** Additionally, GitHub collects analytics data such as page visits and information occasionally volunteered by our users (such as communications with our support team, survey information and/or site registrations).

ROUTED.answer:
**Does “private” prevent GitHub from using your pasted input to improve AI?**

No. Private repository status alone does not prevent that use. Under the Terms of Service, if you provide private repository content as Input to AI Features, GitHub may use that Input to provide, develop, train, and improve the Service, including AI Features [S2]. Separately, GitHub uses your Inputs to generate Outputs and provide the AI Features, and you grant GitHub and its Affiliates a license to collect and use your Inputs and Outputs to develop, train, and improve AI/ML models unless you opt out or are governed by a GitHub Customer Agreement or volume licensing agreement [S1].

Note the scope limit: this license does not extend to Your Content stored in repositories that are not provided as Input to an AI Feature [S1]. So the trigger is providing the content as Input, not merely storing it privately.

**What changes if you opt out?**

If you opt out through your account settings, GitHub will not collect or use your Inputs and Outputs for those development/training/improvement purposes from the effective date of your opt-out going forward [S1]. The opt-out right applies to this use of private repository content as well [S2].

Limits on the opt-out:
- It applies solely to the use of your Inputs and Outputs as described in Section J.3, and does not apply to the license granted in Sections D.4–D.8 or to Content that is not Input or Output (including Content stored in public repositories) [S1].
- Even without opting out, the license does not permit GitHub or its Affiliates to share your Inputs or Outputs with third-party AI model providers for those providers' own independent model training purposes [S1].

**Not specified in the provided evidence**

The sources do not specify the mechanics of how to opt out (e.g., exact settings path), nor whether opting out affects the AI Feature's availability or functionality for you.

1. **User Notifies GitHub of Changes.** If the user chooses to make the specified changes, they _must_ tell us so within the window of approximately 1 business day. If they don't, we will disable the repository (as described in Step 6). If the user notifies us that they made changes, we will verify that the changes have been made and then notify the copyright owner.

1. **Copyright Owner Revises or Retracts the Notice.** If the user makes changes, the copyright owner must review them and renew or revise their takedown notice if the changes are insufficient. GitHub will not take any further action unless the copyright owner contacts us to either renew the original takedown notice or submit a revised one. If the copyright owner is satisfied with the changes, they may either submit a formal retraction or else do nothing. GitHub will interpret silence longer than two weeks as an implied retraction of the takedown notice.

1. **GitHub May Disable Access to the Content.** GitHub will disable a user's content if: (i) the copyright owner has alleged copyright over the user's entire repository or package (as noted in Step 3); (ii) the user has not made any changes after being given an opportunity to do so (as noted in Step 4); or (iii) the copyright owner has renewed their takedown notice after the user had a chance to make changes. If the copyright owner chooses instead to _revise_ the notice, we will go back to Step 2 and repeat the process as if the revised notice were a new notice.

1. **User May Send A Counter Notice.** We encourage users who have had content disabled to consult with a lawyer about their options. If a user believes that their content was disabled as a result of a mistake or misidentification, they may send us a [counter notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice). As with the original notice, we will make sure that the counter notice is sufficiently detailed (as explained in the [how-to guide](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice)). If it is, we will [post it](#e-transparency) to our [public repository](https://github.com/github/dmca) and pass the notice back to the copyright owner by sending them the link.

1. **Copyright Owner May File a Legal Action.** If a copyright owner wishes to keep the content disabled after receiving a counter notice, they will need to initiate a legal action seeking a court order to restrain the user from engaging in infringing activity relating to the content on GitHub. In other words, you might get sued. If the copyright owner does not give GitHub notice within 10-14 days, by sending a copy of a valid legal complaint filed in a court of competent jurisdiction, GitHub will re-enable the disabled content.

FIXED_DIRECT.answer:
**Who should notify you:** If GitHub blocks or disables a Developer Product for legal or policy reasons, GitHub will work with the Product Provider to notify affected users [S4]. So notification is a coordinated effort between GitHub and the Product Provider, not solely one party.

**Does payment guarantee continued access:** The evidence does not support that payment guarantees access against a policy-based disablement. The Marketplace Terms state that for monthly or yearly plans, purchases are billed in advance and are non-refundable, but that "the service will remain active for the length of the paid billing period" [S1]. However, that provision addresses ordinary billing/cancellation, whereas GitHub separately reserves the right to block or disable a Developer Product for legal or policy reasons [S4]. The provided policies do not expressly reconcile these two provisions or state whether a policy-based disablement overrides the "remain active" language.

**Are you owed a partial refund:** The published policies do not specify refunds for a policy-based disablement. The Marketplace Terms state there will be "no refunds or credits for partial months of service, downgrade refunds, or refunds for months unused" [S1]. Separately, the Developer Agreement places refund responsibility on the Developer toward End Users and states GitHub is not liable for payment of any refund [S2]. The evidence does not address a partial refund owed to an End User when a paid app is disabled mid-term for policy reasons.

For billing questions, concerns, or disputes, the Marketplace Terms direct you to contact GitHub through the GitHub Support portal [S1].

Based on the provided policies:

**Who should notify you:** The evidence does not specify who must notify you when a paid Marketplace app is disabled for a policy reason. The takedown provisions describe GitHub's discretion to remove a Listing from Marketplace and your right to appeal such an action [S5], but they do not state a notification obligation or identify who notifies the customer. The provided published policies do not specify the requested information on this point.

**Does payment guarantee continued access:** The billing provisions state that for monthly or yearly plans, the service "will remain active for the length of the paid billing period" [S1][S3]. However, this appears in the context of refunds and cancellation, and the evidence does not address whether that guarantee survives a policy-based disablement. The takedown provisions separately allow GitHub to remove a Listing from Marketplace at its sole discretion [S5], and the termination provisions allow GitHub to terminate the Developer Agreement if the Developer has breached it or if GitHub is required by law [S4]. The provided policies do not expressly resolve how these provisions interact, so the evidence does not clearly establish that payment guarantees continued access after a policy-based disablement.

**Partial refund:** The Marketplace Terms state that purchases are billed in advance and are "non-refundable," with "no refunds or credits for partial months of service, downgrade refunds, or refunds for months unused" [S1]. The GitHub Terms of Service similarly state that monthly or yearly plans are non-refundable, with no refunds for partial months or unused months, and that "no exceptions will be made" [S3]. Under the Developer Agreement, the Developer—not GitHub—is responsible for specifying refund terms to End Users, and GitHub is not liable for payment of any refund [S2]. On this evidence, a partial refund for the unused portion of the annual term is not provided for.

infringing portion is removed.

1. **User Notifies GitHub of Changes.** If the user chooses to make the specified changes, they _must_ tell us so within the window of approximately 1 business day. If they don't, we will disable the repository (as described in Step 6). If the user notifies us that they made changes, we will verify that the changes have been made and then notify the copyright owner.

1. **Copyright Owner Revises or Retracts the Notice.** If the user makes changes, the copyright owner must review them and renew or revise their takedown notice if the changes are insufficient. GitHub will not take any further action unless the copyright owner contacts us to either renew the original takedown notice or submit a revised one. If the copyright owner is satisfied with the changes, they may either submit a formal retraction or else do nothing. GitHub will interpret silence longer than two weeks as an implied retraction of the takedown notice.

1. **GitHub May Disable Access to the Content.** GitHub will disable a user's content if: (i) the copyright owner has alleged copyright over the user's entire repository or package (as noted in Step 3); (ii) the user has not made any changes after being given an opportunity to do so (as noted in Step 4); or (iii) the copyright owner has renewed their takedown notice after the user had a chance to make changes. If the copyright owner chooses instead to _revise_ the notice, we will go back to Step 2 and repeat the process as if the revised notice were a new notice.

1. **User May Send A Counter Notice.** We encourage users who have had content disabled to consult with a lawyer about their options. If a user believes that their content was disabled as a result of a mistake or misidentification, they may send us a [counter notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice). As with the original notice, we will make sure that the counter notice is sufficiently detailed (as explained in the [how-to guide](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice)). If it is, we will [post it](#e-transparency) to our [public repository](https://github.com/github/dmca) and pass the notice back to the copyright owner by sending them the link.

1. **Copyright Owner May File a Legal Action.** If a copyright owner wishes to keep the content disabled after receiving a counter notice, they will need to initiate a legal action seeking a court order to restrain the user from engaging in infringing activity relating to the content on GitHub. In other words, you might get sued. If the copyright owner does not give GitHub notice within 10-14 days, by sending a copy of a valid legal complaint filed in a court of competent jurisdiction, GitHub will re-enable the disabled content.

infringing portion is removed.

1. **User Notifies GitHub of Changes.** If the user chooses to make the specified changes, they _must_ tell us so within the window of approximately 1 business day. If they don't, we will disable the repository (as described in Step 6). If the user notifies us that they made changes, we will verify that the changes have been made and then notify the copyright owner.

1. **Copyright Owner Revises or Retracts the Notice.** If the user makes changes, the copyright owner must review them and renew or revise their takedown notice if the changes are insufficient. GitHub will not take any further action unless the copyright owner contacts us to either renew the original takedown notice or submit a revised one. If the copyright owner is satisfied with the changes, they may either submit a formal retraction or else do nothing. GitHub will interpret silence longer than two weeks as an implied retraction of the takedown notice.

1. **GitHub May Disable Access to the Content.** GitHub will disable a user's content if: (i) the copyright owner has alleged copyright over the user's entire repository or package (as noted in Step 3); (ii) the user has not made any changes after being given an opportunity to do so (as noted in Step 4); or (iii) the copyright owner has renewed their takedown notice after the user had a chance to make changes. If the copyright owner chooses instead to _revise_ the notice, we will go back to Step 2 and repeat the process as if the revised notice were a new notice.

1. **User May Send A Counter Notice.** We encourage users who have had content disabled to consult with a lawyer about their options. If a user believes that their content was disabled as a result of a mistake or misidentification, they may send us a [counter notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice). As with the original notice, we will make sure that the counter notice is sufficiently detailed (as explained in the [how-to guide](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice)). If it is, we will [post it](#e-transparency) to our [public repository](https://github.com/github/dmca) and pass the notice back to the copyright owner by sending them the link.

1. **Copyright Owner May File a Legal Action.** If a copyright owner wishes to keep the content disabled after receiving a counter notice, they will need to initiate a legal action seeking a court order to restrain the user from engaging in infringing activity relating to the content on GitHub. In other words, you might get sued. If the copyright owner does not give GitHub notice within 10-14 days, by sending a copy of a valid legal complaint filed in a court of competent jurisdiction, GitHub will re-enable the disabled content.

ROUTED.answer:
**Who should notify you:** If GitHub blocks or disables a Developer Product for legal or policy reasons, GitHub will work with the Product Provider to notify affected users [S4]. The published policies do not specify a separate direct notification obligation to the end user beyond this.

**Does payment guarantee continued access:** No. The Marketplace Terms state that for monthly or yearly plans, purchases are billed in advance and are non-refundable, but that "the service will remain active for the length of the paid billing period" [S1]. However, this sits alongside GitHub's separate right to block or disable a Developer Product for legal or policy reasons [S4], and the Developer Agreement gives GitHub sole and absolute discretion over what Listings are included on Marketplace, including removal of a Listing [S3]. The provided evidence does not expressly state that payment overrides a policy-based disablement, so continued access is not guaranteed by payment alone.

**Are you owed a partial refund:** The Marketplace Terms state there will be "no refunds or credits for partial months of service, downgrade refunds, or refunds for months unused" [S1]. Separately, the Developer Agreement places responsibility for specifying refund terms on the Developer (Product Provider), and states GitHub is not responsible for providing refund support or liable for payment of any refund [S2]. The provided policies do not specify a partial refund entitlement for a policy-based mid-term disablement.

**Short version:** _We do not generally prohibit use of GitHub for advertising. However, we expect our users to follow certain limitations, so GitHub does not become a spam haven. No one wants that._

While we understand that you may want to promote your Content by posting supporters' names or logos in your Account, the primary focus of the Content posted in or through your Account to the Service should not be advertising or promotional marketing. This includes Content posted in or through Pages, Packages, repositories, and all other parts of the Service. You may include static images, links, and promotional text in the README documents or project description sections associated with your Account, but they must be related to the project you are hosting on GitHub. You may not advertise in other Users' Accounts, such as by posting monetized or excessive bulk content in issues.

You may not promote or distribute content or activity that is illegal or otherwise prohibited by our [Terms of Service](/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service) or [Acceptable Use Policies](/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-acceptable-use-policies), including excessive automated bulk activity (for example, spamming), get-rich-quick schemes, and misrepresentation or deception related to your promotion.

If you decide to post any promotional materials in your Account, you are solely responsible for complying with all applicable laws and regulations, including without limitation the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's Guidelines on Endorsements and Testimonials. FIXED_DIRECT.answer:
GitHub's rules distinguish between promoting Sponsors in your own content and promoting them in other users' spaces:

- **In your own account/Sponsored Developer Content:** You may post Sponsors' names or logos, but the primary focus of that content should not be advertising or promotional marketing [S1][S3]. You may include static images, links, and promotional text in READMEs or project descriptions, but they must relate to the project you host on GitHub [S3].
- **In other users' issue threads:** You may not advertise in other users' accounts, such as by posting monetized or excessive bulk content in issues [S3]. This is the line your proposed cross-promotion in other users' issue threads would cross.
- **Additional limits:** You may not enter an advertising agreement to promote a product or brand if it would violate the Agreement or Community Guidelines [S1], and you may not promote illegal or prohibited content or activity, including excessive automated bulk activity (e.g., spamming) [S3]. If you host promotional materials, you are solely responsible for complying with applicable laws, including the U.S. FTC Guidelines on Endorsements and Testimonials [S1][S3]. GitHub reserves the right to remove promotional materials that violate its terms or policies [S3].

The provided policies do not specify further details on how GitHub enforces these limits in individual cases.

FIXED_DIRECT.raw_query: I normally live outside a trade-restricted region, but my account was flagged while I was traveling through one. Have I permanently lost access to my private repositories, and what can I do if the flag is mistaken?
FIXED_DIRECT.rewritten_query: If my GitHub account was flagged while traveling through a trade-restricted region, have I permanently lost access to my private repositories, and what can I do if the flag is mistaken?

evidence.text:
### How are organization accounts impacted?

If an organization is based out of, or the key individuals or membership of an organization shows sufficient ties to, a sanctioned territory or country for which GitHub does not yet have a license from the U.S. government, or if the organization otherwise appears to be subject to U.S. economic sanctions, then the organization account and the affiliated owner account will be restricted.

The restriction suspends access to private repository services and paid services, such as availability of free or paid private repositories, secret gists, paid Action minutes, Sponsors, and GitHub Marketplace services. For paid organizational accounts associated with such sanctioned regions, users may have limited access to their public repositories, which have been downgraded to archived read-only repositories. For free organizational accounts associated with such sanctioned regions, users will continue to have full access to free public repositories for open source projects (and associated public Pages), public gists, and allotted free Action minutes.
evidence.title: GitHub and Trade Controls

evidence.text:
### How is GitHub ensuring that folks not living in and/or having professional links to the sanctioned countries and territories still have access or ability to appeal?

In the rare instance that an account is affected unintentionally or in error, we have an appeal process to address such instances.

If an individual user or organization owner believes that they have been flagged in error, then that user has the opportunity to appeal the flag by providing verification information to GitHub. If GitHub receives sufficient information to verify that the user or organization is not affiliated with a U.S.-sanctioned jurisdiction for which we do not have a license or otherwise restricted by U.S. economic sanctions, then the flag will be removed. Please contact [Support](https://support.github.com/request) for assistance.
evidence.title: GitHub and Trade Controls
heading_path: How is GitHub ensuring that folks not living in and/or having professional links to the sanctioned countries and territories still have access or ability to appeal?

evidence.text:
### Under the license GitHub has received from OFAC, which types of accounts will be available in Iran?

The license we have secured includes all public and private services, for individuals and organizations, both free and paid.

For example, a developer in Iran may sign up for a Free or Pro plan for their individual use, and an Iranian university may set up an organization account to collaborate with students.

Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs), other denied or blocked parties under U.S. and other applicable law, and certain government officials may be restricted from accessing or using GitHub.

If GitHub determines that an individual or organization falls into a restricted category (SDNs, other blocked parties, or certain government officials), their account will be flagged and they will not be able to use any GitHub features. If they believe that they have been flagged in error, then they have the opportunity to appeal the flag by providing verification information to GitHub. Please contact [Support](https://support.github.com/request) for assistance if needed. If GitHub receives sufficient information to verify that the individual is not in a category restricted by U.S. economic sanctions, then the flag will be removed.
evidence.title: GitHub and Trade Controls
heading_path: Under the license GitHub has received from OFAC, which types of accounts will be available in Iran?

evidence.text:
### What is available and not available?

GitHub now has a license from OFAC to provide cloud services to developers located or otherwise resident in the U.S.-sanctioned country of Iran. The license includes all public and private services for individuals and organizations, both free and paid. GitHub cloud services, both free and paid, are also generally available to developers located in Cuba.

GitHub is committed to continuing to offer free public repository services to developers with individual and organizational accounts in Crimea and the separatist areas of Donetsk and Luhansk. This includes limited access to free services, such as public repositories for open source projects (and associated public Pages), public gists, and allotted free Action minutes, for personal communications only, and not for commercial purposes.

For paid organizational accounts in these sanctioned regions, users may have limited access to their public repositories, which have been downgraded to archived read-only repositories. For free organizational accounts in these sanctioned regions, however, users will continue to have full access to free public repositories for open source projects (and associated public Pages), public gists, and allotted free Action minutes.

GitHub will continue advocating with U.S. regulators for the greatest possible access to code collaboration services to developers in sanctioned regions, including private repositories. We believe that offering those services advances human progress, international communication, and the enduring U.S. foreign policy of promoting free speech and the free flow of information.

Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs), other denied or blocked parties under U.S. and other applicable law, and certain government officials may be restricted from accessing or using GitHub, wherever located. Users may not use GitHub.com for or on behalf of such parties, generally including the governments of sanctioned countries.

GitHub services are not available to developers located or otherwise resident in North Korea.
evidence.title: GitHub and Trade Controls
heading_path: What is available and not available?

evidence.text:
### Can trade-restricted users’ private repositories be made public?

Free individual account users can make restricted private repositories public, for personal communications only, and not for commercial purposes. Users can do this by navigating to the repository settings tab and clicking the "make public" button. Once the repository is public, users have access to public repositories services. This action cannot be undone.
evidence.title: GitHub and Trade Controls
heading_path: Can trade-restricted users’ private repositories be made public?

FIXED_DIRECT.answer:
The provided policies do not say that a trade-control flag is permanent. They describe restrictions and an appeal path, but they do not state that access to private repositories is permanently lost.

- A restriction can suspend access to private repository services and paid services [S1].
- If an account is affected unintentionally or in error, GitHub has an appeal process; the user can provide verification information, and if GitHub receives sufficient information to verify the user is not affiliated with a sanctioned jurisdiction for which GitHub lacks a license or is otherwise restricted, the flag will be removed [S2].
- Similarly, if GitHub determines an individual or organization falls into a restricted category, the account is flagged and cannot use GitHub features, but they may appeal by providing verification information; if GitHub verifies they are not in a restricted category, the flag will be removed [S3].
- For assistance, the policy directs users to contact Support [S2][S3].

So, based on the provided evidence, you have not been told that access is permanently lost; the published policy provides an appeal process for mistaken flags [S2][S3]. The sources do not specify a timeline, outcome guarantee, or any special rule for someone flagged while merely traveling through a restricted region.

### How are organization accounts impacted?

If an organization is based out of, or the key individuals or membership of an organization shows sufficient ties to, a sanctioned territory or country for which GitHub does not yet have a license from the U.S. government, or if the organization otherwise appears to be subject to U.S. economic sanctions, then the organization account and the affiliated owner account will be restricted.

The restriction suspends access to private repository services and paid services, such as availability of free or paid private repositories, secret gists, paid Action minutes, Sponsors, and GitHub Marketplace services. For paid organizational accounts associated with such sanctioned regions, users may have limited access to their public repositories, which have been downgraded to archived read-only repositories. For free organizational accounts associated with such sanctioned regions, users will continue to have full access to free public repositories for open source projects (and associated public Pages), public gists, and allotted free Action minutes.

The license we have secured includes all public and private services, for individuals and organizations, both free and paid.

For example, a developer in Iran may sign up for a Free or Pro plan for their individual use, and an Iranian university may set up an organization account to collaborate with students.

If they believe that they have been flagged in error, then they have the opportunity to appeal the flag by providing verification information to GitHub. evidence.text:
## What are Appeals and Reinstatements?

Both Appeals and Reinstatements may arise in relation to decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account, including decisions whether or not to:

* Remove, disable access to, or restrict visibility of content
* Suspend or terminate access to an account
* Suspend or terminate access to the service, in whole or in part
* Suspend, terminate or otherwise restrict the ability to monetize content

A “Reinstatement” is where a user wishes to regain access to their account or content and is willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation and agrees not to violate our terms going forward.

An “Appeal” is where a user disputes that a violation has occurred and can provide additional information to show that a different decision should have been reached.
evidence.title: GitHub Appeal and Reinstatement

evidence.text:
### Legal Rights

If you believe that a final decision made on Appeal is still incorrect you may, in certain circumstances, have additional rights to seek review of the decision under your local law. For example, if you are located in the European Union, it might be possible to access an out-of-court dispute settlement process under the [Digital Services Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj#d1e2819-1-1). This process reflects GitHub's commitment to internationally recognized human rights set out in the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), privacy, and free expression.
evidence.title: GitHub Appeal and Reinstatement

evidence.text:
### Appeals

Where a user seeks to dispute a decision, they can use the form to explain their basis for disputing the decision and to provide any additional information regarding the alleged violation that they believe should have led to a different decision.

If the information provided demonstrates that a different conclusion should have been reached, we may be able to grant an Appeal. GitHub will reverse or modify its decision when the Appeal contains sufficient grounds for us to determine that (i) our decision to act or not to act was mistaken; (ii) that the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with our Terms; or (iii) that the content or conduct warrants a lesser severity of action than the measure taken.

All decisions on Appeal are made by humans and not by any automated means. If the GitHub Staff reviewer on the Appeal is the same person who made the initial determination and that staff member believes their initial conclusion was correct (and thus would be inclined to deny the Appeal), a different member of GitHub’s staff will independently review the Appeal.

All legitimate Appeals will be answered with a final decision.
evidence.title: GitHub Appeal and Reinstatement

evidence.text:
## Can I open a support ticket to recover my account?

For security reasons, **GitHub Support will not restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you lose your two-factor authentication credentials or lose access to your account recovery methods.** You must use existing [account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials).

GitHub does not support any other means of account recovery, including social or ID verification, by members of GitHub’s staff. This policy is in place to protect your account from unauthorized access through social engineering.
evidence.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
heading_path: Can I open a support ticket to recover my account?

FIXED_DIRECT.answer:
No. The two are governed by different commitments, and responsibility for the Marketplace app's access to your data rests primarily with the app's developer, not GitHub.

**Subprocessor on the list**
- The GitHub Subprocessor List identifies vendors authorized to subprocess customer or personal data *on behalf of GitHub* to provide services to Enterprise customers, and applies to GitHub services governed by the GitHub Data Protection Agreement [S1].
- GitHub uses such vendors for services on its behalf, and they are bound by contractual obligations to ensure the security, privacy, and confidentiality of your information [S2].

**Marketplace app**
- For third-party applications available on the Marketplace, GitHub may share Personal Data *upon your instruction*, and **you are responsible for the data you instruct GitHub to share with these applications** [S2].
- The developer is solely responsible for its Developer Products, and GitHub has no responsibility or liability of any kind for any aspect of them [S4][S5].
- The developer's Data Protection Addendum requires it to ensure any third party it engages provides at least the same level of privacy protection, to process Personal Data only for permitted purposes, and makes the developer directly liable to GitHub for actual damages caused by breach of that Addendum [S3].

**Bottom line**
- A subprocessor is a vendor acting on GitHub's behalf under GitHub's data-processing commitments [S1][S2].
- A Marketplace app is a third-party product you instruct GitHub to share data with; the developer is solely responsible for the product and its data handling, and you are responsible for the data you direct GitHub to share [S2][S4][S5].

The provided published policies do not specify whether a Marketplace app is itself covered by the GitHub Data Protection Agreement; the evidence addresses the developer's separate data protection obligations under the Marketplace Developer Agreement [S3].

FIXED_DECOMPOSE.answer:
No. The evidence treats subprocessors and Marketplace apps as different relationships with different responsibility allocations.

**Subprocessors**
- The Subprocessor List identifies vendors authorized to subprocess customer or personal data *on behalf of GitHub* to provide services to Enterprise customers, and applies to GitHub services governed by the GitHub Data Protection Agreement [S1].
- GitHub states it uses vendors to provide services on its behalf and that those vendors are bound by contractual obligations to ensure the security, privacy, and confidentiality of your information [S2].

**Marketplace apps**
- For third-party applications available on the Marketplace, GitHub states that *upon your instruction* it may share Personal Data with them, and that **you are responsible for the data you instruct GitHub to share with these applications** [S2].
- The Marketplace Developer Agreement places responsibility on the Developer: the Developer is solely responsible for its Developer Products [S5], must protect End Users' privacy and legal rights, provide a legally adequate privacy notice and protection, obtain valid consent as required, and comply with applicable data privacy obligations [S4]. The Developer must also ensure any third party it uses provides at least the same level of privacy protection [S3], and is directly liable to GitHub for actual damages caused by breach of the Data Protection Addendum [S3].
- The EULA governing an End User's rights to a Developer Product is solely between Developer and End User, and GitHub has no responsibility or liability under it [S5].

**Bottom line**
- A subprocessor on GitHub's list is engaged by GitHub under GitHub's data-processing commitments [S1][S2].
- A Marketplace app is a third-party Developer Product: GitHub shares data with it on your instruction, you are responsible for that instruction [S2], and the Developer bears its own privacy, consent, and liability obligations [S3][S4][S5].

The provided published policies do not specify whether a Marketplace app is itself covered by the GitHub Data Protection Agreement; the evidence addresses subprocessors under that agreement [S1] and Marketplace apps under the Marketplace Developer Agreement and Privacy Statement [S2][S3][S4][S5].

# Addendum 1: Data Protection Addendum

This Data Protection Addendum (this “Addendum”) is attached to and made a part of the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement between you and GitHub (the “Agreement”). Terms not defined in this Addendum have the meanings ascribed to them in the Agreement. In the event of a conflict or inconsistency, the terms of this Addendum will supersede those of the Agreement.

**A1-1. Purpose and Scope**
GitHub maintains Personal Data from individuals all over the world, some of whom are residents of countries and areas with strong data protection laws. This Addendum establishes your responsibilities when you receive and process any such Personal Data from GitHub.

**A1-2. Definitions**

* (a) “Applicable Data Protection Laws” means any laws, regulations, regulatory frameworks, or other legislations relating to the processing and use of Personal Data, as applicable to the Agreement, including:
   * The EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (“GDPR”), along with any implementing or corresponding equivalent national laws or regulations;
   * The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, Cal. Civ. Code §§1798.100 et seq. ("CCPA"); and
   * The UK Data Protection Act 2018 and implementation of GDPR contained therein.
* (b) “Personal Data” means any information which relates to an individual GitHub End User, customer or employee which could, alone or together with other information, identify them, whether supplied by GitHub for processing by the Developer or whether generated by the Developer in the course of performing its obligations under this Agreement.
* (c) “Processing” means any operation or set of operations performed on Personal Data, whether by manual or automatic means, including collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, blocking, erasure, or destruction.

**A1-3. Compliance with Data Transfer Laws**

* (a) GitHub Compliance. GitHub complies with Applicable Data Protection Laws. GitHub relies on Standard Contractual Clauses ("SCCs") for all transfers out of the European Union, European Economic Area, United Kingdom, and Switzerland to provide its services. GitHub also complies with the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (EU-U.S. DPF), the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF, and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (Swiss-U.S. DPF) as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce. GitHub has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (EU-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of Personal Data received from the European Union in reliance on the EU-U.S. DPF and from the United Kingdom (and Gibraltar) in reliance on the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF. GitHub has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (Swiss-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of Personal Data received from Switzerland in reliance on the Swiss-U.S. DPF.
* (b) Developer Compliance. Developer represents and warrants that it will (i) comply with Applicable Data Protection Laws; and (ii) abide by the requirements of European Economic Area and Swiss data protection laws regarding the collection, use, transfer, retention, and other processing of Personal Data from the European Economic Area, United Kingdom, and Switzerland.

ROUTED.answer:
No. The evidence treats these two categories differently.

**Subprocessor on GitHub's list**
- The GitHub Subprocessor List identifies vendors authorized to subprocess customer or personal data *on behalf of GitHub* to provide services to Enterprise customers, and it applies to all GitHub services governed by the GitHub Data Protection Agreement [S1]. GitHub also commits to publishing new subprocessors at least 30 days before they are authorized to perform services that may involve access to customer or personal data [S1]. Separately, GitHub states that vendors used to provide services on its behalf are bound by contractual obligations to ensure the security, privacy, and confidentiality of your information [S2].

**Marketplace app**
- Marketplace apps are addressed under a different framework. GitHub states that, upon your instruction, it may share Personal Data with third-party applications available on its Marketplace, and that **you are responsible for the data you instruct GitHub to share with these applications** [S2].
- The Marketplace Developer Agreement places responsibility on the Developer: the Developer is solely responsible for its Developer Products [S5], and must protect End Users' privacy and legal rights, provide a legally adequate privacy notice and protection, obtain valid consent as required, and comply with applicable data privacy obligations [S4]. The Developer's Data Protection Addendum also requires the Developer to ensure any third party it engages provides at least the same level of privacy protection, restricts processing to permitted purposes, and makes the Developer liable to GitHub for actual damages caused by breach of that Addendum [S3]. The EULA for a Developer Product is solely between Developer and End User, and GitHub has no responsibility or liability under it [S5].

**Bottom line**

# Addendum 1: Data Protection Addendum

This Data Protection Addendum (this “Addendum”) is attached to and made a part of the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement between you and GitHub (the “Agreement”). Terms not defined in this Addendum have the meanings ascribed to them in the Agreement. In the event of a conflict or inconsistency, the terms of this Addendum will supersede those of the Agreement.

**A1-1. Purpose and Scope**
GitHub maintains Personal Data from individuals all over the world, some of whom are residents of countries and areas with strong data protection laws. This Addendum establishes your responsibilities when you receive and process any such Personal Data from GitHub.

**A1-2. Definitions**

* (a) “Applicable Data Protection Laws” means any laws, regulations, regulatory frameworks, or other legislations relating to the processing and use of Personal Data, as applicable to the Agreement, including:
   * The EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (“GDPR”), along with any implementing or corresponding equivalent national laws or regulations;
   * The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, Cal. Civ. Code §§1798.100 et seq. ("CCPA"); and
   * The UK Data Protection Act 2018 and implementation of GDPR contained therein.
* (b) “Personal Data” means any information which relates to an individual GitHub End User, customer or employee which could, alone or together with other information, identify them, whether supplied by GitHub for processing by the Developer or whether generated by the Developer in the course of performing its obligations under this Agreement.
* (c) “Processing” means any operation or set of operations performed on Personal Data, whether by manual or automatic means, including collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, blocking, erasure, or destruction.

**A1-3. Compliance with Data Transfer Laws**

* (a) GitHub Compliance. GitHub complies with Applicable Data Protection Laws. GitHub relies on Standard Contractual Clauses ("SCCs") for all transfers out of the European Union, European Economic Area, United Kingdom, and Switzerland to provide its services. GitHub also complies with the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (EU-U.S. DPF), the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF, and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (Swiss-U.S. DPF) as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce. GitHub has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (EU-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of Personal Data received from the European Union in reliance on the EU-U.S. DPF and from the United Kingdom (and Gibraltar) in reliance on the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF. GitHub has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (Swiss-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of Personal Data received from Switzerland in reliance on the Swiss-U.S. DPF.
* (b) Developer Compliance. Developer represents and warrants that it will (i) comply with Applicable Data Protection Laws; and (ii) abide by the requirements of European Economic Area and Swiss data protection laws regarding the collection, use, transfer, retention, and other processing of Personal Data from the European Economic Area, United Kingdom, and Switzerland.
